<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
This PKGBUILD is safe for the narrow gate of `makepkg --nobuild --nodeps --noprepare` and `makepkg --printsrcinfo`.

The top-level code consists of variable assignments, arch detection (`_upstream_arch`), URL template construction, and source array definitions. The `printf` invocations inside command substitutions (`$(printf "${_url}" 20260822075341 i386)` and `$(printf "${_url}" 20260822075321 x86_64)`) simply format a URL string by substituting a Wayback Machine timestamp and architecture into the template `https://web.archive.org/web/%dif_/https://eidas.minv.sk/downloadservice/eidklient/linux/eID_klient_%s.tar.gz`. This is a standard, legitimate use of the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine to access archived versions of the official Slovak eID client download. `printf` does not download or execute anything; it only produces a string that is stored in the source arrays.

There is no `pkgver()` function, no `eval`, no base64 decoding, no piped downloads, and no other commands at the top level or in source definitions that would execute anything dangerous. The `: "${var[@]}"` no-op statements merely reference variables. `prepare()` and the two `package_*()` functions are out of scope for this gate since they won't run with `--noprepare` and `--nobuild`.

The `sha256sums` array uses SKIP for the four local source files (eidklient, patch-qt, qt.hook, qt6.conf), which is standard for non-downloaded sources. The architecture-specific tarballs have real SHA-256 checksums, which is good hygiene.
</details>
<evidence>

<security_assessment>
<decision>SAFE</decision>
<details>
This is a standard pacman `.install` file for the eidklient (Belgian eID client) AUR package. It contains routine pre/post-install and pre/post-remove/upgrade hooks.

The `checkpcscd()` function simply checks whether the pcscd service is enabled and prints a helpful message if not — this is standard and harmless.

The `pre_install`, `pre_upgrade`, and `pre_remove` hooks only delete files within the application's own install directories (`/opt/eidklient/lib/patched/*` and `/usr/lib/eID_klient/libQt6*`). These are self-scoped cleanup operations, expected when upgrading an application that patches Qt library paths.

The `post_install` and `post_upgrade` hooks execute `/opt/eidklient/patch-qt`, which is a script shipped and installed by the package itself (it is part of the application's own functionality, used to fix Qt library loading). Running a script that the package just installed is a normal packaging pattern.

There are no network requests, no data exfiltration, no obfuscation, no execution of downloaded code, and no manipulation of files outside the application's own scope.
</details>
<evidence>

However, the file paths are specified using HTML-escaped entities (") instead of actual double quotes. This results in invalid arguments being passed to objcopy (e.g., "/usr/lib/libQt6Core.so.6"), causing the command to fail. As written, the script cannot execute the intended operation and poses no security risk. There is no evidence of malicious behavior such as data exfiltration, obfuscation, unauthorized network activity, or execution of attacker-controlled code. The script's purpose appears to be a legitimate (though incorrectly quoted) binary patching operation.
</decision>
